summary: Psalm 147 calls Jerusalem and Israel to praise Yahweh because he restores the city, gathers outcasts, heals the wounded, counts the stars, and upholds the humble. The poem moves from praise for God's care of the lowly, to thanksgiving for rain and food, to praise from Jerusalem for peace, provision, weather, and the gift of his word to Israel.
whyItMatters: This psalm stands near the end of the Psalter, where the collection gathers into repeated calls to praise. It shows praise grounded in specific claims: restoration, creation's order, daily provision, protection, and God's revealed ordinances.

context.author: Anonymous within the chapter; Psalms is a many-writer anthology, and not every psalm can be assigned to one author with certainty.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping community, especially addressed here as Jerusalem, Zion, Jacob, and Israel.
context.date: Psalms contains material from different periods, and assigning one date to the whole collection would be misleading; this chapter itself speaks of Jerusalem being built up and Israel's outcasts gathered.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, within the closing cascade of praise psalms that lead the collection toward total praise.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew praise poetry, using repeated calls to praise and paired lines that move between God's care for people, creation, weather, and his word.

outline.heading: Praise for restoration and care
outline.note: The psalm opens by saying praise is good, pleasant, and fitting, then names Yahweh as builder of Jerusalem, gatherer of outcasts, healer of the broken, counter of stars, supporter of the humble, and judge of the wicked.

outline.heading: Thanksgiving for rain and food
outline.note: A second call to sing turns to God's care for the sky, rain, mountains, livestock, and young ravens.

outline.heading: What Yahweh delights in
outline.note: The poem contrasts military or human strength with those who fear Yahweh and hope in his loving kindness.

outline.heading: Jerusalem's security and provision
outline.note: Jerusalem and Zion are summoned to praise because God strengthens gates, blesses children, gives peace, and fills the city with wheat.

outline.heading: God's word over weather
outline.note: God's command and word move swiftly through the earth, bringing snow, frost, hail, cold, wind, melting, and flowing waters.

outline.heading: God's word to Israel
outline.note: The psalm closes by distinguishing God's word, statutes, and ordinances shown to Jacob and Israel, ending again with praise.

keyVerses.text: Praise Yah, for it is good to sing praises to our God; for it is pleasant and fitting to praise him.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the psalm's main action and its reason: praise is presented as good, pleasant, and fitting.

keyVerses.text: He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the psalm's concern for wounded people, not only for the rebuilt city or the ordered creation.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his loving kindness.
keyVerses.why: This verse explains what kind of human response the psalm says delights Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: He shows his word to Jacob, his statutes and his ordinances to Israel.
keyVerses.why: Near the end, the psalm turns from God's word governing the weather to God's word given to Israel.

themes: care for the broken and humble
God's rule over creation and weather

questions.question: Who is being called to praise in this psalm?
questions.answer: The opening call is broad: “Praise Yah” and “sing praises to our God.” Later the poem addresses Jerusalem and Zion directly, and it names Jacob and Israel near the end. The chapter therefore sounds like communal praise, with Jerusalem and Israel especially in view.

questions.question: What does “Praise Yah” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “Praise Yah” is the command that opens and closes the poem. “Yah” is the shortened divine name used in the hosted text, and the chapter expands that command by listing reasons for praise.

questions.question: Does the chapter say Jerusalem has already been restored?
questions.answer: The psalm says, “Yahweh builds up Jerusalem” and “gathers together the outcasts of Israel.” It does not give a date or narrate the rebuilding process. Readers often connect this language with restoration after disaster or exile, but the chapter itself presents it as a reason for praise rather than a detailed history.

questions.question: Why does the psalm move from broken hearts to stars?
questions.answer: The poem places intimate care and cosmic knowledge side by side. Yahweh heals the broken in heart, and he also counts and names the stars. The movement suggests that the same God who governs what seems vast also attends to wounded people.

questions.question: What kind of strength does the psalm reject?
questions.answer: The psalm says Yahweh does not delight in the strength of the horse or take pleasure in the legs of a man. In the next verse, it says he takes pleasure in those who fear him and hope in his loving kindness. The contrast is between visible power and reverent dependence, though the chapter does not develop that into a full political theory.

questions.question: Is the weather language just scenery?
questions.answer: No. Snow, frost, hail, cold, wind, and flowing waters are part of the psalm's account of God's command in the earth. The weather images show God's active rule over creation, not merely a background for human life.

questions.question: Why mention livestock and young ravens?
questions.answer: The psalm says God provides food for livestock and for young ravens when they call. That widens the scope of praise beyond Jerusalem's human community. God's care is pictured as reaching ordinary animals and vulnerable creatures.

questions.question: Is verse 20 saying other nations have no value?
questions.answer: Verse 20 says God has not shown his ordinances to “just any nation,” and that “They don’t know his ordinances.” The point in the chapter is Israel's distinctive reception of God's word, statutes, and ordinances. Readers differ on how to relate this claim to later Jewish and Christian discussions of the nations, but the verse itself is focused on the privilege and responsibility of Israel receiving God's instruction.

glossary.def: The command that frames the psalm, calling the community to praise God.
The city named as being built up by Yahweh and later directly summoned to praise.
The scattered or displaced people of Israel whom the psalm says Yahweh gathers together.
The quality in which the faithful hope; the psalm links it with fearing Yahweh.
God's instructions or rulings shown to Israel, named alongside his word and statutes.
